The skills that matter most to this user are ones they build themselves with the skill-creator skill for proprietary workflows, such as writing a service in their back-testing framework. For niche tools like marimo, they have a deep-thinking agent research up front and condense it into a skill, so the agent doesn't waste time and context rediscovering it every session.
Critique: "At least MCPs can be unit tested. With Skills however, you just selectively append more text to prompt and pray."

Concern that unrestricted free-form Markdown, even with YAML frontmatter, makes skills inherently hard to evaluate. The user wants agents to be systematically evaluable, and free-text instructions don't lend themselves to that.

For database access, one user built a small MCP script with listTables, getTableSchema and executeQuery, which blocks DROP and DELETE, instead of using a skill: "I wouldn't trust a textual instructions to prevent LLMs from dropping a table." Another user's workaround is simply giving the LLM a read-only connection.

One user describes a Metabase skill for querying analytics that uses progressive disclosure: it only pulls in authentication instructions when the agent isn't already authenticated. Other practical skills they use: writing tests, fetching Sentry info, using Playwright, and submitting PRs per team conventions. They say "a lot of local mcps are just flat out replaced by skills."

Skills are "much better than MCP, which also stuffs every session's precious context with potentially irrelevant instructions." The same user later argues custom tooling instructions still consume more context than letting the LLM use standard tools it already understands.

Workflow: whenever you correct the agent on something it did wrong, ask it to revise the relevant .md file or skill so the correction sticks. Content starts as sections in agents.md and graduates to a separate skill file once it gets large enough. The index is just a short paragraph per file, so it's token efficient.
Because skills are a semi-special construct, agents are better at leveraging them when needed. You can also invoke them explicitly, e.g. "use the PR skill to open a PR."
Skills suit longer context you don't always want loaded, such as a debugging methodology or designing data schemas. If you always want something in context, use rules/memories instead.
A user who had been raving about Claude Skills said they were excited to see skills come to Codex as well.
